draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Pichavaram! You're at the edge of one of the largest mangrove forests in India, about 45 square km of islands and channels where the trees stay rooted in a few feet of water. A sand bar is all that keeps it apart from the Bay of Bengal.
draft.hungryLine: Pichavaram is a small village, so carry snacks and water for your boat trip, and save the proper meal for Chidambaram, 15 km away.

moodReplies.show-me-around: The Pichavaram Boathouse is just a 3 min walk away, the starting point for gliding through the mangrove channels. The Watch Tower is right next to it for a view from above.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Climb the Watch Tower, 3 minutes on foot, and look out over the islands and water of the Killai backwater.
moodReplies.surprise-me: These mangroves sit between two river mouths, the Vellar estuary to the north and the Coleroon to the south, which together form the Killai backwater.

spots.name: Pichavaram Boathouse
spots.detail: 3 min walk · Hop on a boat into the mangrove channels

spots.name: Watch Tower
spots.detail: 3 min walk · A high view over the mangrove islands

tips.title: Go early.
tips.body: Head out on the water in the morning before the coastal sun gets strong.

tips.title: Base yourself in Chidambaram.
tips.body: Chidambaram is just 15 km away and has plenty of places to eat and stay.

story.title: Two rivers meet the sea
story.body: The Vellar and Coleroon rivers reach the sea on either side of Pichavaram. Their estuaries form the Killai backwater, where the mangroves took root.

story.title: Parangipettai's coast
story.body: Pichavaram is one of the villages of Parangipettai, long a major trading centre on the Coromandel Coast, especially for Arab and Yemeni traders. The Portuguese, Dutch and English later took turns colonising the area.

story.title: A huge mangrove forest
story.body: The Pichavaram mangroves covered about 45 square km, with trees like Avicennia and Rhizophora. They also shelter rare shells and fish that local people depend on.

story.title: Planting for the future
story.body: Tamil Nadu has been planting mangroves in Cuddalore district and nine other districts. The aim is to soften cyclones, tidal surges and coastal erosion while supporting wildlife and local livelihoods.
